name: Sooke

facts.text: We could not confirm from the District's website whether Sooke has adopted a municipal tree-cutting bylaw; the District surveyed residents on a proposed tree management bylaw in 2020. Check with the District of Sooke before removing large trees. Inside development permit areas (foreshore, riparian, steep slopes and others), vegetation removal is regulated through the OCP; see sooke-ocp-800-dpas.
facts.sourceTitle: Sooke survey collects thoughts on tree bylaw - Sooke News Mirror
facts.excerpt: Sooke council is working on a bylaw to regulate tree management.
facts.note: V2 UNVERIFIED (status note, NOT a claim that no bylaw exists). Checked: the District's Bylaws page (/municipal-hall/bylaws/) lists Burning, Noise, Parking and Securing Attractants regulation pages and no tree page; the Urban Forest and Tree Care page gives care advice and describes no tree-cutting permit. The 'Browse and Search Bylaws' list loads only through a scripted search, which was not run this session, so the full bylaw register was not seen. The news article (SECONDARY, 2020) was not re-fetched (host not allowed).

facts.text: Most of Sooke's tree canopy is on private land. The District's tree-care guidance tells owners to water young trees for their first 2-3 years, prune dead or damaged branches ideally in the dormant season, and hire a certified arborist for large or complex work.
facts.sourceTitle: Urban Forest and Tree Care - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Most of Sooke’s tree canopy is on private land.
facts.note: V2: new. Same page, verbatim: 'Hire a certified arborist for large or complex work.' Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: Sooke is a forested community, and the District's FireSmart landscaping advice is to keep 1-1.5 m of non-combustible space around the home, keep shrubs and woody debris tidy and well spaced from 1.5 to 10 m out, prune branches up to 2 m from the ground, and keep trees at least 10 m from structures where possible. Sooke Fire Rescue Services (250-642-5422) books free home and property assessments.
facts.sourceTitle: Urban Forest and Tree Care - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Call Sooke Fire Rescue Services at 250-642-5422 to book a free home and property assessment.
facts.note: V2: the source is now the District's own page, replacing the SECONDARY CTV article; the program is current. Correction: added the District's FireSmart zone guidance; dropped 'sooke.ca/firesmart', which returned 404 on the District host. Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: Sooke adopted Official Community Plan Bylaw No. 800 on December 8, 2025. Its Part 7 sets out nine development permit areas: Energy and Water, General, Foreshore Area, Riparian Area, Steep Slopes, Town Centre, Intensive Residential, Neighbourhood Commercial and Employment Lands. Inside them, land alteration, building and subdivision need a development permit unless an exemption applies, and a DPA Viewer map shows which may apply to a property.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: issuance of a Development Permit is required prior to any proposed land alteration, building and subdivision within a DPA.
facts.note: V2: Correction: the adopted plan has NINE DPAs (DPA 1-9), not the '10 DPAs' Capital Daily reported for the DRAFT. The OCP page (https://www.sooke.ca/programs-services/planning-and-development/official-community-plan-ocp/), verbatim: 'On December 8, 2025, Council adopted Official Community Plan (OCP) Bylaw No. 800 (PDF)'. There is no separate wildfire DPA; Part 7 can require a wildfire hazard assessment for lands over 4 ha. The PDF was fetched from the District's Govstack media host, the same host as the earlier sourceUrl.

facts.text: Sooke's OCP exempts yard or garden work within an existing landscaped area from development permits. It also exempts planting native trees, shrubs or groundcover to improve habitat or soil stability, and removing invasive plants (such as gorse, Scotch broom, knotweed, English ivy and daphne) by low-disturbance hand or mechanical methods, as long as native plants go back in right away.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: Yard or garden work within an existing landscaped area;
facts.note: V2: new (s.7.1.2 xiv, xv, xvii). The invasive-removal exemption, verbatim, requires 'immediate replacement with vegetation native to the surrounding ecosystem'.

facts.text: In Sooke's permit areas, removing hazardous trees is exempt only with an ISA Certified Arborist's report accepted by the District beforehand. In riparian and foreshore areas, the removal must also be supervised or confirmed by a Qualified Environmental Professional.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: In riparian or foreshore Development Permit Areas, hazardous tree removal must be supervised or confirmed by a Qualified Environmental Professional (QEP)
facts.note: V2: new (s.7.1.2 xxiv).

facts.text: Sooke's Foreshore Area permit area deals with grading, vegetation removal or structural works within about 15 m of the sea's natural boundary. It is not meant to regulate routine maintenance or gardening in existing yards, and its guidelines ask that existing trees and native vegetation be kept within at least 15 m upland of the shore.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: The intent is not to regulate routine property maintenance, gardening, or enjoyment of existing residential yards
facts.note: V2: new (s.7.4.1 and guideline viii, 'Retain existing trees and native vegetation within a minimum of 15 metres upland').

facts.text: Sooke's Steep Slopes permit area (DPA 5) covers mapped parcels and any land with slopes over 30% across at least 10 m horizontally. Land clearing and other site disturbance there is reviewed to protect slope stability and properties downhill.
facts.sourceTitle: OCP Bylaw No. 800, Part 7 - Development Permit Areas (District of Sooke)
facts.excerpt: have slopes greater than 30% for a minimum horizontal distance of 10m.

facts.text: Backyard burning in Sooke is allowed only from November 1 to April 30, when the ventilation index is Good, no fire ban is in place and the weather is safe. Under Fire Protection Services Bylaw No. 292, burning yard waste or clearing land needs a permit from Sooke Fire Rescue, and fires must be at least 15 m from buildings and property lines. As an alternative, the District runs free yard-waste drop-off in May at the Sooke Parks Yard, 2070 Kaltasin Road.
facts.sourceTitle: Burning Regulations - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Backyard burning is permitted in the District of Sooke from November 1 to April 30, when ventilation is GOOD and conditions are safe.
facts.note: V2: the source is now the official District page, replacing the SECONDARY Island Social Trends post; the season dates are confirmed. Added from the page FAQ, verbatim: 'open burning beyond small recreational fires—including yard waste burning, land clearing, or larger fires—requires a permit issued by Sooke Fire Rescue.' The page's opening text and its FAQ differ on whether basic backyard burning needs a permit; tell readers to call Sooke Fire Rescue first. Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: Sooke's priority invasive plants include knotweed, English ivy, Himalayan blackberry, Scotch broom, gorse, giant hogweed and garden escapees such as lamium, daphne and periwinkle. The District works with the T'Sou-ke Nation on knotweed along salmon streams and warns never to cut or compost knotweed or to compost any invasive plant.
facts.sourceTitle: Invasive Species - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Do not cut or compost: Cutting promotes regrowth and spreads fragments.
facts.note: V2: new official replacement for the invasive-species angle of sooke-scotch-broom. Same page, verbatim: 'Never compost invasive plants; dispose of them according to guidelines, such as those provided by the CRD.' Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: Scotch broom is said to have reached Vancouver Island through an 1851 Sooke garden, and it still crowds rural Sooke lots; the District has run an annual broom drop-off at its parks yard.
facts.sourceTitle: Sooke wants you to pull some broom - Times Colonist (May 5, 2024)
facts.excerpt: Sooke wants you to pull some broom
facts.note: V2 UNVERIFIED: SECONDARY and not re-fetched (host not allowed). The District's invasive page lists Scotch broom as a priority species but does not mention 1851 or a broom drop-off; the burning page mentions a free yard-waste drop-off in May only. Use sooke-priority-invasives instead.

facts.text: The District says bears, cougars, deer, raccoons and other wildlife commonly move through Sooke neighbourhoods, especially in spring and fall. Gardens and fruit trees draw them in, and deer need space in fawning season.
facts.sourceTitle: Coexisting with Wildlife - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: It’s common to see bears, cougars, deer, raccoons, and other wildlife moving through neighbourhoods, especially in spring and fall.
facts.note: V2: new; closes the R1b deer gap for Sooke (no deer-management program found, just the District's guidance). Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: Sooke's Animal Regulation and Impounding Bylaw No. 392 requires residents to secure wildlife attractants, which it says include compost, fruit trees and fallen fruit. The District advises harvesting fruit promptly, clearing fallen fruit, and fencing or netting where appropriate.
facts.sourceTitle: Securing Attractants - District of Sooke
facts.excerpt: Under Bylaw No. 392, residents must ensure attractants are secured.
facts.note: V2: new. Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: Sooke is on the CRD's Juan de Fuca water system (see regional-crd-water-systems), but some rural properties beyond the mains are reported to rely on wells or hauled water, and council has backed extending service to about 75 Otter Point Road properties. Confirm a property's supply before planning irrigation.
facts.sourceTitle: Sooke council backs water service extension - Sooke News Mirror
facts.excerpt: Sooke council backed extending municipal water to about 75 properties on Otter Point Road
facts.note: V2 PARTLY VERIFIED: the CRD Drinking Water Systems page confirms that the Juan de Fuca system serves Sooke (reviewed in regional-crd-water-systems). The wells, hauled-water and Otter Point extension claims are still SECONDARY and were not re-fetched (host not allowed). The excerpt is a search snippet and is undated.

facts.text: The District of Sooke notes that fall and winter storms bring higher tides, strong winds and storm surges to Sooke's coastline, washing driftwood, seaweed and debris onto the Whiffin Spit trail.
facts.sourceTitle: Storm Surges and High Tides Bring Seasonal Changes to Whiffin Spit - District of Sooke (Nov 16, 2026)
facts.excerpt: As fall and winter storms bring higher tides, strong winds and storm surges to Sooke's coastline
facts.note: V2: the source is now an official District bulletin dated Nov 16, 2026, replacing Wikipedia. Correction: removed the Wikipedia-only claims (the spit 'almost landlocks' the harbour, breakwater repairs). Any 'exposed waterfront lots' framing is ours. Page fetched via sooke-012-ca.govstack.com, the District of Sooke's own Govstack host that serves the same site as www.sooke.ca (www.sooke.ca itself was refused by this session's network).

facts.text: CRD Stage 1 watering rules (Water Conservation Bylaw No. 4099) run May 1 to September 30 every year for properties on the Regional Water Supply System: lawns may be watered two days a week by address (even: Wednesday and Saturday; odd: Thursday and Sunday), 4-10 am or 7-10 pm by any method, or 12:01-10 am or 7-10 pm with timed/automatic irrigation. Trees, shrubs, flowers and vegetable gardens may be sprinkled any day 4-10 am or 7-10 pm, and hand watering or micro/drip irrigation is allowed any day, any time. Strata and other multi-unit complexes use the complex's street address. New sod and newly seeded lawns need no permit and have a temporary schedule.
facts.sourceTitle: Regional Watering Schedule - Capital Regional District
facts.excerpt: Stage 1 Watering Schedule of the Water Conservation Bylaw No. 4099 for the Regional Water Supply System is in effect May 1 through September 30 every year.
facts.note: V2: verified on the live CRD page (www.crd.ca/node/4919 redirects here). Corrections: added the separate timed/automatic irrigation window (12:01-10 am or 7-10 pm), the any-day rules for trees, shrubs and gardens, the multi-unit address rule and the bylaw number. Shared regional block, not municipality-specific; R1a files use the id 'crd-watering-stage1' for the same rule, so the integrator should merge the two ids.

facts.text: The CRD's Juan de Fuca Water Distribution System supplies drinking water to Colwood, Langford, Metchosin, View Royal, Sooke, parts of Highlands and East Sooke; the Saanich Peninsula Water Distribution System supplies Central Saanich, Sidney and North Saanich. Properties not connected (for example on private wells) are outside the CRD watering schedule.
facts.sourceTitle: Drinking Water Systems - Capital Regional District
facts.excerpt: The Juan de Fuca Water Distribution System provides drinking water to Colwood, Langford, Metchosin, View Royal, Sooke, parts of Highlands and electoral area East Sooke.
facts.note: V2: new shared regional fact. Same page, verbatim: 'The Saanich Peninsula Water Distribution System provides drinking water to Central Saanich, Sidney and North Saanich.' The last sentence (unconnected properties are outside the schedule) follows from the watering page, which says Bylaw 4099 applies to customers of the Regional Water Supply System.

facts.text: Invasive plants can be taken to Hartland Landfill in bags marked 'Invasive Species' or in covered loads; knotweed needs a controlled waste permit and must not go to municipal yard-waste drop-offs. The CRD's Regional Invasive Species Program lists priority species including giant hogweed, knotweed, gorse, poison hemlock, shiny geranium and yellow toadflax.
facts.sourceTitle: Invasive Species - Capital Regional District
facts.excerpt: Invasive species can be disposed of at Hartland Landfill. They must be in bags marked “Invasive Species” or in covered loads.
facts.note: V2: new shared regional fact; it confirms the CRD invasive-species note already used in content/areas/*.json. Same page, verbatim: 'Knotweed species disposal requires a controlled waste permit (reduced fee)' and 'Note: Knotweed species must not be disposed of at these locations.'

facts.text: B.C.'s riparian rules (the Riparian Areas Protection Regulation, formerly the Riparian Areas Regulation) apply across the Capital Regional District except the City of Victoria and Esquimalt. Residential, commercial or industrial work within 30 m of a fish-bearing stream, lake, wetland or ditch, including removing or altering plants and disturbing soil, can need a Qualified Environmental Professional's assessment; each local government sets how it applies through permit areas or bylaws. Amendments to the regulation take effect January 1, 2027.
facts.sourceTitle: Riparian Areas Regulation brochure (Province of B.C., 2016)
facts.excerpt: within 30 metres of a watercourse, even if that watercourse is not on your property,
facts.note: V2: the 30 m figure is not on the RAPR web page itself, so the source is now the provincial brochure. Brochure, verbatim: the activities listed include 'Removing or altering plants' and 'Disturbing soils'. Regulation page (https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/environment/plants-animals-ecosystems/fish/aquatic-habitat-management/riparian-areas-regulation), verbatim: 'Amendments to RAPR come into effect on January 1, 2027.' Citizen resources page (.../riparian-areas-regulation/citizen-resources), verbatim: 'Capital (except City of Victoria and Esquimalt)'. The 2016 guidebook adds that the rules do not apply to marine or estuarine shorelines. The brochure predates the 2019 rename and the 2027 amendments, so re-check after January 1, 2027.

facts.text: Section 34 of B.C.'s Wildlife Act makes it an offence to take, injure, molest or destroy a bird or its egg, the nest of an eagle, peregrine falcon, gyrfalcon, osprey, heron or burrowing owl (protected even when not in use), or any other bird's nest while it holds a bird or egg. Trees are therefore checked for nests before felling or heavy pruning, especially in spring and summer.
facts.sourceTitle: Migratory Birds and Breeding Birds: Federal and Provincial Legislation (BC Timber Sales, March 2024)
facts.excerpt: possesses, takes, injures, molests or destroys: a) A bird or its egg, b) The nest of an eagle, peregrine falcon, gyrfalcon, osprey, heron or burrowing owl
facts.note: V2: the earlier source (www2.gov.bc.ca .../environmental-regulatory-compliance/wildlife) now returns 404, so the source is now this provincial guidance sheet, which quotes section 34. Same sheet, verbatim: 'c) The nest of a bird not referred to in paragraph (b) when the nest is occupied by a bird or its egg.' It also says inactive nests of listed species 'have regulatory protection'. Correction: the species list is now exact (peregrine falcon, gyrfalcon and burrowing owl added; 'some other nests' removed).
